title: Reylo Type Defs 0.1.0
description: What introspecting one SQL statement returns, and the type descriptor of each parameter and column in it: which values the position can hold, across relational databases. The format's reference is at https://reylo.dev/typedefs.

Type.description: A type descriptor: which values a position can hold. Every kind, from everyday to advanced; a union lists its members in this order, and a new kind is appended, so the order never changes.

name.description:
The database's name for the type, less the modifiers a field states: `numeric` for `numeric(10,2)`, but `tinyint(1)` for MySQL's `BOOLEAN`, whose `(1)` bounds no value. It is in the dialect the document states once at its top. When a schema defines the type, the name is qualified, and it is the type's identity.
  - Postgres: `int4`, `varchar`, `timestamptz`, `public.mood` (an enum), `public.email` (a domain), `public.vector` (an extension's type).
  - MySQL: `bigint`, `enum`, `json`.
  - SQLite: the declared type the value traces to, through `max`, `coalesce` and union arms too.
  - Oracle: `VARCHAR2`, `R.SHAPE_T`.

Absent on a type the statement builds, such as the record inside a `json_build_object`. It never changes what the type means. Generators and drivers key their conventions on it, such as MySQL's `tinyint(1)` as a boolean.

comment.description: The comment the database keeps on a named type: `COMMENT ON TYPE` or `COMMENT ON DOMAIN`. A column's own comment is on the column.

Bounds.description: Bounds on an ordered kind's values, in its canonical text (`"-1.50"`, `"2026-10-23"`, and for a decimal an exponent where it is shorter, `"1e126"`), as JSON Schema's `minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum` and `exclusiveMaximum` are: each holds a value, so `CHECK (x > 0)` on a float is `exclusive_min: "0"`. A side takes one of its two fields. A whole-number kind takes only `min` and `max` (`x > 0` is `min: "1"`); any other kind writes a bound as the constraint states it, so `x > 0` on a `numeric(10,2)` is `exclusive_min: "0"`, never `min: "0.01"`. Bounds constrain the finite values only: whether infinity, -infinity and NaN also occur is said by the `infinity` and `nan` flags alone, whatever the bounds.

Size.description: How long a value is, in whole numbers of its kind's unit (bytes, elements, or a text's own `unit`): `exact`, or `min`, `max` or both, never `exact` beside either. `char(8)` is `size: { exact: 8 }`, `varchar(255)` is `size: { max: 255 }`, and Oracle's `VARCHAR2(20 CHAR)`, which stores `''` as null, is `size: { min: 1, max: 20 }`. A length is never exclusive, since a whole number has an inclusive spelling.

BooleanType.description: A truth value: Postgres `boolean`, SQL Server `bit`, Oracle `BOOLEAN`, and a comparison's result on any database, which MySQL and SQLite deliver as 1 or 0. A MySQL `BOOLEAN` column is an `integer`, since it can hold 5.

IntegerType.description: A whole number of a fixed width, two's complement unless `unsigned`: `int4` is 32 bits, MySQL `BIGINT UNSIGNED` 64 bits unsigned, SQL Server `tinyint` 8 bits unsigned, MySQL `MEDIUMINT` 24 bits, DuckDB `HUGEINT` 128 bits, SQLite `INTEGER` 64 bits, and Vertica's `TINYINT`, despite its name, 64 bits. Its range follows from the width; bounds narrow it further, from a CHECK or for a type narrower than any width, as MySQL `YEAR` (0 and 1901 to 2155, 16 bits bounded at 0 and 2155). A whole-number bound is always written inclusive, since `x > 0` is `x >= 1`. An integer of no fixed width is a `decimal` whose scale is at most 0.

unsigned.description: From 0 to 2^bits − 1: MySQL `UNSIGNED`, SQL Server `tinyint`, Postgres `oid`.

enum.description: The only values, as JSON Schema's `enum`: a `CHECK (x IN (…))`, or a constant the statement writes (`select 1 as one`).

FloatType.description: An IEEE 754 binary float, given by its exponent and mantissa widths, which fix its range and precision: `float8`, SQLite `REAL` and SQL Server `float` are 11 and 52, `float4` 8 and 23, the half float in pgvector's `halfvec` 5 and 10, and ClickHouse's `BFloat16` 8 and 7. A width alone would not do, since those last two are both 16 bits. A generator picks the smallest native float whose widths are both at least these. -0 is a float like any other, and equal to 0.

mantissa_bits.description: Not counting the implicit leading bit.

infinity.description: Also holds infinity and -infinity: Postgres's floats, SQLite's `REAL`. MySQL's `FLOAT` and `DOUBLE` refuse them.

nan.description: Also holds NaN: Postgres's floats. SQLite stores a NaN as NULL, and MySQL refuses it.

DecimalType.description:
An exact decimal: `numeric`, MySQL `DECIMAL`, Oracle `NUMBER`, `DECFLOAT`. It is a kind of its own, so that a generator switching on the kind never turns money into `int64` or `double`.

A decimal is a coefficient, a whole number, times a power of ten: 1.25 is 125 × 10^-2. IEEE 754 and the General Decimal Arithmetic specification call the coefficient's digits the precision and the power the exponent; SQL and Java's `BigDecimal` count the exponent negated, as the scale, the digits after the point. A type bounds both:
  - `numeric(10,2)`: precision 10, scale 2, so up to 99,999,999.99. MySQL `DECIMAL(M,D)`, SQL Server `decimal(p,s)` and Oracle `NUMBER(p,s)` alike, and SQL Server `money` is (19,4) with bounds at -922,337,203,685,477.5808 and 922,337,203,685,477.5807. Oracle's `NUMBER(5,-2)` has scale -2, rounding to hundreds.
  - Postgres `numeric` with no size: scale 0 to 16,383, below 10^131072 in magnitude.
  - `DECFLOAT(34)`, IEEE's decimal128: precision 34, scale -6111 to 6176.
  - Oracle `NUMBER`: precision 40, below 10^126 in magnitude; Oracle `INTEGER` adds a scale of at most 0.

A decimal is a number, so 1.5 and 1.50 are one value however the database prints them. Postgres `money` is `opaque`: its scale follows the session's locale, and the client receives `$1,234.57`.

precision.description: The most digits in the coefficient.

min_scale.description: A value is in the type when it can be written as a coefficient of at most `precision` digits times 10^-scale, with a scale from `min_scale` to `max_scale`: so `numeric(5,2)`, precision 5 and scale 2 to 2, holds 1.5, written 150 × 10^-2. Equal bounds make a fixed scale.

infinity.description: Also holds infinity and -infinity: Postgres `numeric` with no size, `DECFLOAT`. Java's `BigDecimal`, Rust's `rust_decimal` and C#'s `decimal` hold neither, nor NaN.

nan.description: Also holds NaN: Postgres `numeric`, sized or not, `DECFLOAT`.

TextType.description: Text is one kind in three shapes, by whether every value is valid Unicode (well-formed, in the Unicode Standard's word, which JavaScript's `isWellFormed()` uses too). A length counts in a unit, since languages disagree on what a string's length is: four code points take 4 to 16 bytes in UTF-8, and a JavaScript string's `length` counts UTF-16 units. A shape takes only the units that mean something for its values. How text compares, under a collation, is not part of its type, since a collation adds and removes no value.

UnicodeText.description: Valid Unicode: Postgres, MySQL and Oracle text. Its lengths count code points (`varchar(255)` is `size: { max: 255 }`), UTF-16 units (Oracle `NVARCHAR2`), or bytes in the encoding the database stores it in (MySQL `TEXT` is `size: { unit: "byte", encoding: "UTF-8", max: 65535 }`). `char(8)` is `size: { exact: 8 }`, since Postgres pads it with spaces.

TextSize.description: A valid text's size, which says what it counts: code points when `unit` is absent, UTF-16 units, or bytes in `encoding`.

encoding.description: The encoding bytes are counted in, written only with `unit: "byte"`.

IllFormedUtf8Text.description: Bytes meant as UTF-8 but never validated, so a value may not be valid Unicode: SQLite `TEXT` (`CAST(x'ff' AS TEXT)`), ClickHouse `String`, a Postgres `SQL_ASCII` database, Firebird `NONE`. A JavaScript string cannot hold every value. Its lengths count bytes, and its patterns are `like` and `ilike`, since a regular expression matches characters.

IllFormedUtf16Text.description: UTF-16 units that may hold a lone surrogate: SQL Server `nvarchar`, `nchar` and `ntext`. A Rust `String` cannot hold every value. Its lengths count UTF-16 units.

pattern.description: A pattern every value matches, in its own dialect and matched as that dialect matches: `like` and `ilike` against the whole value, a regular expression anywhere in it unless anchored. A case-insensitive match (`~*`, or `REGEXP` under a case-insensitive collation) begins its source with `(?i)`. Postgres's and ECMA's regular expressions disagree on `.` and newlines.

enum.description: The only values, as JSON Schema's `enum`: a database's enum type (Postgres `create type mood as enum (…)`, MySQL `ENUM(…)`), a `CHECK (x IN (…))`, or a constant the statement writes (`select 'user' as kind`). An enum type's declared order concerns only how its values sort, so it is not part of the type.

BytesType.description: Bytes: `bytea`, `binary(n)` (exactly n), `varbinary(n)`, `BLOB`, `RAW(n)`, SQL Server `rowversion` (8), Postgres `macaddr` (6) and `macaddr8` (8).

UuidType.description: A 128-bit identifier (RFC 9562): Postgres `uuid`, SQL Server `uniqueidentifier`, MariaDB `UUID`.

ArrayType.description:
A sequence of `element`s, in order. Where its index starts is not part of the type.
  - **Nesting:** a two-dimensional array is an array of arrays. A Postgres array column takes `any_depth`, since Postgres ignores declared dimensions: one `int[]` column holds `{1,2}` and `{{1,2},{3,4}}`. Every array a statement builds (`array_agg`, `ARRAY[…]`, a JSON array) has the depth its nesting shows.
  - **Its size** counts the outermost array's elements. A fixed shape, such as DuckDB's `INTEGER[3]` or a 3×3 matrix, is arrays of exact sizes, nested.
  - **A vector** is an array of floats: pgvector's `vector(3)` is exactly 3 elements, and MySQL's `VECTOR(n)` at most n.
  - **A bit string** is an array of booleans: Postgres `bit(7)` and MySQL `BIT(7)` are exactly 7, and Postgres `varbit(n)` at most n. That is its value, not its representation: a client may hold one as a string of 0s and 1s, a number or a buffer.

any_depth.description: An element may itself be an array of `element`, to any depth, each value rectangular.

JsonType.description:
A JSON value: `json`, `jsonb`, MySQL `JSON`.
  - `content`: what the statement built (`json_build_object`, `json_agg`), described with the same types. Each leaf is typed by the SQL value the database wrote it from: inside a `json_build_object`, an `int8` may pass 2^53, which a JSON Schema could not say.
  - `schema`: a JSON Schema every value satisfies, from a CHECK or a parameter's typed cast, whose `$schema` names the draft it is read by: MySQL's `JSON_SCHEMA_VALID` reads draft 4, and Postgres's validator extensions differ.
  - Neither: any JSON, whose numbers may have any length (`jsonb` keeps them as `numeric`), never only doubles.

What each database writes for each type is in "Facts about each database".

DateType.description: A calendar date. Postgres's runs from `-4713-11-24` to `+5874897-12-31`, in astronomical years.

infinity.description: Also holds infinity and -infinity, which sort after and before every other value, whatever the bounds, which constrain only finite values.

TimeType.description: A time of day: `time(p)`. Postgres's holds `24:00:00` itself, its `max`, which Java's `LocalTime`, Python's `time` and Temporal refuse. With `zone`, each value keeps an offset too: Postgres `timetz`.

DateTimeType.description: A date and time of day as a wall clock reads, with no zone: Postgres `timestamp`, MySQL `DATETIME`, SQL Server `datetime2`, Oracle `DATE`.

infinity.description: Also holds infinity and -infinity, which sort after and before every other value, whatever the bounds, which constrain only finite values.

InstantType.description: A point on the timeline: Postgres `timestamptz`, MySQL `TIMESTAMP`, Oracle `TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE`. Each stores the moment and shows it in the session's zone. Bounds are in UTC.

zone.description: Absent: only the moment, with no claim about any offset, as Postgres `timestamptz`, which takes `12:00+05:30` and gives back that moment in the session's zone.

infinity.description: Also holds infinity and -infinity, which sort after and before every other value, whatever the bounds, which constrain only finite values.

Zone.description: What each value keeps besides the moment: a UTC offset (SQL Server `datetimeoffset`, Postgres `timetz`), a region such as `America/Los_Angeles`, or either, per value (Oracle `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`, Firebird's `WITH TIME ZONE` types). No database keeps regions alone today.

DurationType.description:
A length of time, in the parts it has (months, days and time), each signed on its own. A month and a day have no fixed length (a month is 28 to 31 days, and a day 23 to 25 hours across a clock change), so a duration that counts them keeps them apart from its time: Postgres adds `1 month` to January 31 as February 28, and `1 day` across a clock change as 23 or 25 hours.
  - Postgres `interval` has all three (`1 mon -1 day`, which `Temporal.Duration` refuses): `P2147483648M2147483648DT2562047788H54.775808S`.
  - Oracle's `INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH` has months alone (`P1199M`), and its `INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND` time alone (`PT2399H59M59.999999S`), since it holds a day as 24 hours.
  - MySQL `TIME` is time alone: `PT838H59M59S`.

SQL calls this kind an interval; ISO 8601's intervals are a start and an end, which is a `range` here.

max.description: The parts its values have, each at the largest magnitude it reaches, of either sign, as one ISO 8601 duration: months in `M`, days in `D`, then time in `H`, `M` and `S`, its minutes and seconds below 60. A part the type lacks is left out, and a part it has is never 0. A two's complement part reaches one unit further below zero than above it, so it is written at the negative side's magnitude: Postgres's months reach -2147483648 and +2147483647, and are `2147483648M`.

tick.description: The time part's smallest step, written exactly when `max` has a time part.

infinity.description: Also holds infinity and -infinity: Postgres's, from version 17.

UnionType.description:
One of several types: each value is one of them. A SQLite column that is not STRICT holds what its affinity stores, an object column with subtypes holds any subtype's record, and MySQL's `:n + 1` is a BIGINT, a DOUBLE or a DECIMAL by what is bound and how the driver sends it. A union whose members a database names, and whose values say which member they are, is a `tagged_union`.

A union of no members holds no value, so a position typed so with `nullable` is always null: the field of a `json_build_object('a', null)`.

SetType.description: Elements in no order, each at most once by the element type's equality: MySQL `SET`, a set of the values it declares, at most 64. A client may receive the elements in any order. Not an array, since it has no rank and no index.

duplicates.description: An element may appear more than once, making a multiset: the SQL standard's `MULTISET`, Oracle's nested tables.

MapType.description: Keys to values, each key once by the key type's equality, in no order: `hstore` (text to nullable text). A key is never null. A map whose keys may repeat, such as ClickHouse's `Map`, is an array of `{ key, value }` records.

RangeType.description: A range of `subtype`, with an empty range and unbounded ends: Postgres ranges, Teradata `PERIOD`, and ISO 8601's intervals, a start and an end. Its subtype is any type the database orders, which on Postgres takes in an array, a composite and a `boolean`. Over a discrete subtype, such as integers or dates, `[1,3]` and `[1,4)` are one range. An unbounded end lies beyond the subtype's infinities, so `[x,)` holds infinity and `[x,infinity)` does not.

MultirangeType.description: An ordered set of non-overlapping ranges: Postgres multiranges.

GeometryType.description: An OGC simple feature: PostGIS `geometry` and `geography` (`geodetic`), and the spatial types of MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle.

XmlType.description: XML: a document with one root, valid against any `schemas` given, or a fragment, which may have several roots (`<a/><b/>`), as Postgres's `xml` may. An XML Schema validates documents only, so a fragment names none.

OpaqueType.description: A type the database knows and the format does not structure: an extension's own, such as Postgres `ltree`, `tsvector` and `pg_lsn` or SQL Server's `hierarchyid`, and Postgres `money`, whose scale follows the session's locale. Its `name` is all the format says; what a value looks like is the driver's to decide.

AnyType.description: The database's own type admits a value of any type, each carrying its type, which is one of this format's types: SQL Server `sql_variant`, Oracle `ANYDATA`.

UnknownType.description: Nothing is known about the values.

TaggedUnionType.description: One of several alternatives, each named by the tag every value carries, in the order the type declares them: DuckDB's `UNION(num INTEGER, str VARCHAR)`, a Rust enum. Unlike a union's members, two alternatives may hold one type, and a value says which alternative it is, even where it holds NULL (DuckDB's `union_value(num := NULL)` is no NULL union).

Alternative.description: An alternative of a tagged union: its tag, unique in the type, and the value it holds.

StatementDescriptor.description: What introspecting one statement returns. A tool may write keys of its own beside these, as `reylo compile` writes the file a statement was read from.

$schema.description: The version of the format the descriptor is written in, as the URL of that version's JSON Schema, which a validator or an editor reads. Versions are semantic, and until 1.0.0 a new minor version may change anything.

sql.description: The statement as the database runs it, with its own placeholders (`$1` on Postgres, `?` on MySQL and SQLite), in the order `params` lists them.

kind.description: `select` for any query, a `VALUES` list and a set operation included; `other` for any statement that is none of the five: a `CALL`, whose procedure may write, an `EXPLAIN`, a `SHOW` or a SQLite `PRAGMA`, and DDL. Absent when the statement does not parse.

comment.description: The prose written in comments before the statement: its summary, as an editor's hover shows it.

columns.description: In order; empty when the statement returns no rows.

cardinality.description: How many rows the statement returns: exactly one, at most one, any number, or none (a write without `RETURNING`).

diagnostics.description: What the database or the introspection reports against the statement, each at its place, so an editor can underline it. A statement that does not parse has a diagnostic and no columns.

Diagnostic.description: `start` and `end` are offsets into the statement as it was written, in UTF-16 units, as the Language Server Protocol counts by default. `code` is the database's own error code where it has one (Postgres's SQLSTATE `42703`, MySQL's `1054`).

Position.description: Where a value stands: a column, a parameter, a record's field, an array's element, a map's value, or JSON content. Nullability lives here, never in a type, since an outer join makes any position nullable whatever its type.

nullable.description: The value may be null; absent, it never is. On a parameter, the statement accepts null; inside JSON content, the value may be JSON null.

Column.description: A result's column. A row always has every column, so none is optional. A row is an object keyed by its columns' names, which keeps only the last of two with one name, so a statement whose result repeats a name (`select a.id, b.id`) has a diagnostic at each later column of it, asking for another name with `as`.

name.description: The name the database gives the column: Postgres calls `select 1`'s `?column?`, and SQL Server leaves it empty.

comment.description: The comment the database keeps on the column (`COMMENT ON COLUMN`).

optional.description: The key may be absent: a structured parameter's `?` member, a JSON object's key (as `jsonb_strip_nulls` drops). Apart from `nullable`, and never a default value.

Param.description: A statement's parameter. Where the statement writes it whole into a column, its type is that column's: `insert into t (price) values (:price)`, into a `numeric(10,2)` column, gives `price` precision 10 and scale 2, though Postgres describes the parameter as plain `numeric` and would round 1.234. That is stricter than the server, never looser.

optional.description: The caller may leave the parameter out.

comment.description: The comment the database keeps on the column the parameter is written to whole.

Dialect.description: The database a document of descriptors describes, stated once at the document's top: every `name` inside is this dialect's. `name` is the database's, such as `postgres`, `mysql`, `sqlite`, `oracle` or `sqlserver`, and `version` its server version.
